note: Byte budgets for everything shipped to a browser or embedded in a document. A `derivative` budget is built with sharp at check time from the real original, because no derivative is committed. A `client-js` budget is read out of the real `next build`, so it needs `pnpm --filter @berelax/web build` first — CI runs that before this step and scripts/test-gates.mjs asserts the ordering. A `video` budget measures whatever the hero video job last wrote into the fake storage outbox, and always checks that its number is the one the pipeline itself enforces — so a budget with nothing to measure still fails when the two disagree.

budgets.label: Design tokens stylesheet
budgets.why: Loaded on every page and inlined into every generated document. It is 21 colours and five scales; a token layer past 6KB has stopped being a token layer.

budgets.label: Tailwind theme
budgets.why: A mapping, not a stylesheet. Growth here means utilities are being defined where components should be.

budgets.label: Fonts embedded in every generated PDF
budgets.why: Four woff2 subsets carried by every invoice. docs/08 budgets 120KB Latin and 100KB Arabic for the web; a document pays both at once, and a fifth face would put 40KB on every emailed invoice.

budgets.label: A one-page tax invoice
budgets.why: Emailed to customers and kept for five years of FTA retention. Most of it is the font subsets; a sharp rise means an image or a second font crept in.

budgets.label: A one-page tax invoice, Arabic-primary
budgets.why: The heaviest of the six M-TILL-12 documents: the full field set, three lines, and the Arabic-primary render, which draws more of the Arabic face than the English one. Most of the file is the four font subsets, so a sharp rise means an image, a fifth face or an embedded logo crept onto a document that is emailed to customers and kept for five years of FTA retention.

budgets.label: A one-page simplified invoice, Arabic-primary
budgets.why: Budgeted below the full form on purpose: the simplified invoice drops the customer block and two columns, so if it ever costs as much as the tax invoice then something is being rendered that its field list does not declare.

budgets.label: A one-page receipt, Arabic-primary
budgets.why: The form issued most often — every walk-in gets one — and the shortest. The floor is the embedded fonts, so this budget is really a fence around the document furniture.

budgets.label: Client JS every route ships
budgets.why: docs/08 §7: the motion library lives in "≤2 code-split islands, never in the shared layout". This is the shared layout, measured — the chunks every route in the application loads before any page of its own. Two things make "zero bytes attributable to motion" checkable rather than asserted. The allow-list catches a motion island, or anything else, becoming a client reference the whole site pays for: a new name here fails by rule name. And the number catches what a module list cannot see, because a library imported *inside* an allowed module is bundled into that module's chunk and appears nowhere as a module of its own — motion v12 is 32-36KB gzip, and this budget has under 3.5KB of room. The two modules that are allowed are the theme and the direction provider, both of which exist because localStorage and Radix portals cannot be read on the server.

budgets.label: The two motion islands
budgets.why: docs/08 §7 budgets each island at "roughly 32-36KB gzip (UNVERIFIED)" for the motion library, and W-SYS-04 caps an island at 40KB gzip. Measured over the chunk that *defines* the islands rather than the chunk group loaded with them, because Turbopack gives every client module on a route the same chunk list and a shared list cannot be divided between its modules. Both islands land in one chunk today, so this one number is the stronger reading of "each island": if the pair is inside the per-island budget, either alone is. The wider question — a library joining an island's import graph and being put in a chunk of its own — is the kitchen-sink route budget below, and neither measurement replaces the other.

budgets.label: Client JS the kitchen sink adds
budgets.why: Everything the route with the most client code on it loads beyond the shared layout: the Radix dialog, popover and select (about 31KB gzip of the total, and W-SYS-09's note about the primitives barrel is why they are on this route at all), Next's own dynamic-import helpers, and the motion islands at under a kilobyte. It is the number that moves when a library arrives anywhere in an island's graph rather than in the island's own chunk, which is exactly what a `motion` import would do — 32-36KB gzip against about 7KB of headroom. docs/08 §8 budgets first-party JS on the home route at 110KB gzip; the home route ships none of this, and this dev surface is deliberately the worst case on the site.

budgets.label: The hero video attach island
budgets.why: docs/08 §6 budgets "a ~1.4KB island" to attach the hero video after LCP, and W-SYS-07's acceptance holds it to ≤2KB gzip. Measured over the chunk that DEFINES the module, the same narrow reading as the two motion islands above — Turbopack gives every client module on a route the same chunk list, so a chunk list cannot be divided between the modules that share it. The number is what makes the design checkable rather than asserted: the whole point of this island is that the hero costs ~0ms LCP and a kilobyte or two of deferred JavaScript, and an island that quietly grew a library would still work, still pass every behavioural test, and cost what the video hero was supposed to save. `[missing-client-module]` is the vacuity guard in the other direction: a budget over a module no route ships measures zero bytes and passes forever, which is exactly how a check stops being one (ADR 0003).

budgets.label: Screenshot gallery page
budgets.why: It references its captures rather than embedding them. Inlining took it to 24MB once the specimen carried photographs, over the Artifact limit; this budget is what notices if that returns.

budgets.label: Hero poster, AVIF, widest mobile rung
budgets.why: docs/08 §8: the LCP element on a phone. 95KB is affordable only because this photography is soft and low-detail; a high-contrast replacement needs 140-180KB for the same perceptual quality, and the first thing that tells us is this number. The other three heroes are measured in packages/fixtures/src/media-derivatives.itest.ts; one hero here keeps `pnpm budgets` to two encodes.

budgets.label: Hero video, 4:5 mobile rendition
budgets.why: docs/08 §8: "Hero video (deferred, gated) ≤350KB" on a phone, where the budget bites and where docs/08 §8's cut order drops video to the still first. It is enforced in two places on purpose. Here it is a CI failure with the measured number — the second of docs/08 §8's three enforcement layers. In the job it is not: the job refuses only at the 2MB hard stop, because a job that refused at the budget would make the hard stop a rule that can never fire, and docs/08 §8's cut order is the documented route back under budget rather than a gate.

budgets.label: Hero video, 16:9 desktop rendition
budgets.why: docs/08 §8: "≤1.2MB — hard stop 2MB". 1.2 × 1048576 rounded, matching the KiB basis of every other budget in this file. The heaviest single thing the site serves, and the only one that is deferred until after LCP — docs/08 §6 puts its LCP cost at 0ms because the element has no src until LCP is final, which is what makes a megabyte of decoration affordable at all.

budgets.label: Hero poster, AVIF, widest desktop rung
budgets.why: docs/08 §8, the heaviest single derivative the site serves. The worst of the four heroes already uses about 90% of this, so it is a live budget rather than a round number.
